data.title: EMEA Morning Briefing: Wall Street Expects Anthropic's Debt to Be Junk
data.description:
MARKET WRAPS

Watch For:

PMI for Eurozone, Germany, U.K., France; No major corporate trading updates expected

Opening Call:

European stock futures traded mixed early Monday. Asian stock benchmarks were lower; the dollar was flat; Treasury yields were unchanged; while oil futures and gold were higher.

Equities:

Stock futures point to a mixed open in Europe, after last week's tumble sparked fears of a Black Monday scenario.

Investors are succumbing to worries over the future of the artificial-intelligence trade despite Anthropic's larger-than-expected initial public offering.

"The latest selloff reflects growing concerns over stretched technology valuations, the scale and financing of AI-related capital expenditure, and uncertainty over the returns on these investments," Commerzbank Research analysts said.

Forex:

Currencies were mixed against the dollar as traders digested divergent signals. On the one hand, higher U.S. stock futures could buoy appetite for risky assets. On the other hand, "hawkish Fed commentary and FOMC minutes have supported the U.S. dollar," StoneX's Matt Simpson said.

Also, "disappointing Chinese economic data has added pressure to industrial metals and other commodities, while AI valuation concerns have weighed heavily on Wall Street and global risk appetite," the senior market analyst added.

Bonds:

Borrowing big in the corporate bond market won't be easy for Anthropic. The debt market expects credit-rating firms to rate its bonds as junk, or below investment grade.

"How do you gauge what the right price is for a company that has committed to spend $900 billion in the next couple of years?" said Craig Manchuck, a bond-fund manager at Osterweis Capital Management.

An investment-grade rating would give artificial-intelligence company access to the $8.6 trillion high-grade corporate bond market, a relief for microchip manufacturers. But several large bond-fund managers said they expect Anthropic to land a rating in the BB range.

Roughly half of the AI lab's spending commitments don't start until 2030. Without an investment-grade rating by then, Anthropic could struggle to pay its bills.

Energy:

Oil fell amid risk-off sentiment spurred by the global equity market selloff on Friday.

"Concerns over the returns generated by AI investment remain at the center of the correction, but weakness has broadened beyond technology," ANZ Research analysts said.

However, oil-price losses might be limited by geopolitical tensions that could lead to supply disruptions. A Russian warship was struck at a Libyan port on Sunday. The Merkury, a Steregushchiy-class corvette, was the second Russian ship hit over the weekend, after a cargo vessel was struck in the Baltic Sea on Saturday.

Metals:

Gold strengthened in a likely technical rebound. The precious metal recorded its biggest weekly decline last week since March as the drag from the rout across the AI sector was compounded by hawkish Federal Reserve signals, ANZ Research analysts said.

The prospect of tighter monetary policy has also kept Treasury yields elevated, with 10-year Treasurys yield hovering around 5%, they note. However, "the decline is now approaching the first major support hurdle, and the focus is on a possible exhaustion low in the weeks ahead," StoneX strategist Michael Boutros said. Copper was lower in Asian trading. Prices are under pressure as a drop in AI stocks raised concerns about future demand for the metal, ANZ research analysts said.

AI development requires massive data centers and upgraded power grids, both of which rely heavily on copper. Investor sentiment was also weighed by a stronger dollar, which makes the metal more expensive for buyers holding other currencies, the analysts said. Iron ore prices lost ground. Demand remained subdued on weak steel-mill profitability, Anliang Futures analysts said. Port inventories continued to build, while steel mills' imported stocks declined, showing winter restocking has yet to start, they added.

Elevated inventories also weighed on prices, while improving producer prices provided some support, they said. Investors should watch for macroeconomic policy shifts and the Fed's interest-rate decisions, they said.

TODAY'S TOP HEADLINES

EU Inks Trade Deal With Indonesia to Cut Tariffs, Catalyze Investment

The European Union signed ambitious agreements with Indonesia that eliminate most tariffs on goods between the two sides, aiming to will deliver billions in economic benefits.

Brussels announced the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement with Indonesia on Saturday, more than 10 years after negotiations began. The parties also inked an Investment Protection Agreement to encourage bilateral flows.

The AI Build-Out Is Sucking Up Resources and Crowding Out the Rest of the Economy

The artificial-intelligence build-out has become the major force behind U.S. economic growth. But in doing so it is also pushing other areas of the economy aside.

Anthropic's tumultuous performance dragged down the whole market on Friday, just a day after debuting the largest public offering ever. The selloff, combined with problems at chip maker Nvidia, underscored risks to an economy so dependent on AI for growth.

Two Russian Ships Attacked Far From Ukraine

A Russian warship was struck at a Libyan port on Sunday, the latest in a series of suspected Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian vessels as attacks spread far beyond the battlefield.

The Merkury, a Steregushchiy-class corvette, was the second Russian ship hit this weekend, after a cargo vessel was struck in the Baltic Sea on Saturday. Satellite images showed the warship smoldering and partially submerged in the water at the port city of Benghazi on Libya's Mediterranean coast.

Fugitive Criminals Need a New Hideout Since the U.A.E. Started Extraditing Them

International fugitives have long found refuge in the desert emirate of Dubai, where loose financial regulations and generous visa rules have allowed them to park illicit fortunes and live walled off from criminal investigations in their home countries.

Now, the ground under crime lords hiding out in the United Arab Emirates is shifting.

Anthropic Committed to Spend $900 Billion. Wall Street Expects Its Debt to Be Junk.

Anthropic's stock market debut was rocky. There are even bigger questions about how it will fare in the bond market.

The hot artificial-intelligence company raised more than $100 billion last week and is worth around $1.18 trillion, above Walmart or JPMorgan Chase. But it has committed to spend some $900 billion in the coming years to pay for the gargantuan amount of computing power needed for its leading AI models.

data.title: Tata Steel to Buy Stake in Indian Steel Tubes Maker in Near $1.7 Billion Deal
data.description:
By P.R. Venkat

Tata Steel agreed Monday to buy a 26.6% stake in APL Apollo Tubes for $1.67 billion, paving the way to take control of the smaller Indian steel tubes maker.

Tata Steel will pay 2,100 Indian rupees, equivalent to $22.67, a share for the stake held by APL Apollo's promoters, the steelmaker said in an exchange filing Monday.

Tata Steel will also make an open offer for a further 26% stake at 2,301.40 rupees a share.

On Sunday, Tata Steel agreed to sell its steel tubes business and its coated steel unit, Tata Steel Colors, to APL Apollo for 280 billion rupees.

APL Apollo would fund the acquisition through a mix of acquisition financing and subsequently replace the debt with long-term capitalization to de-risk the balance sheet, the statement said.

After the deal closes, APL Apollo will become Tata Steel's main vehicle for growth in steel tubes and coated steel, with a combined capacity of 7.5 million tons a year.

Tata Steel shares are trading 5.8% lower and APL Apollo is down 15%.

data.title: Asian Regulators Step Efforts to Calm AI-Driven Market Turmoil
data.description:
By Sherry Qin

Regulators and market operators in China, South Korea and Taiwan have rolled out emergency measures to arrest the turmoil sparked by the global rout in artificial-intelligence stocks.

Asian markets remained volatile on Monday, though some improvements suggest the moves could be soothing worries about the unwinding of the AI investment boom.

China's tech-heavy ChiNext index reversed morning declines to gain 1.2% in afternoon trading, while Taiwan's Taiex benchmark also rebounded, last up 2.9%.

South Korea's Kospi pared earlier losses of as much as 5.8% to last sit 3.2% lower.

Asian authorities' efforts to quell volatility come in the wake of the Nvidia scandal that led to Jensen Huang's exit.

Huang's departure spurred a wave of selloffs in AI-related names as investors worried about the unravelling of billions in financing that he orchestrated, and which have underpinned the industry's growth.

A turbulent debut by Anthropic then capped a $4 trillion wipeout in the U.S. last week, moves mirrored in Asia, where Taiwan's Taiex suffered its worst week since 1990. South Korea's benchmark Kospi has lost nearly 18% in the month to date.

South Korea and Taiwan had moved to stem the bleeding in AI and tech shares earlier this month, and are now bulking up market defenses.

In Seoul, officials are preparing a market-stabilization fund and vowed to step up scrutiny of trading activity, including illegal short selling and market manipulation during a three-month period. They will also ease limits on daily share buybacks for three months starting Tuesday.

South Korea's Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il on Monday warned that volatility in the semiconductor sector could amplify fluctuations in the broader economy, noting that external risks remain high amid regulatory uncertainty about AI, geopolitical tensions and rising interest rates.

Taiwan has already activated its own market-stabilization fund, deploying support for local stocks since Nov. 6. Established in 2000, the Taiwanese fund has about $15 billion of capital at its disposal and steps in during times of crisis, like the Covid pandemic.

The island's Financial Supervisory Commission said Saturday that it has tightened short-selling rules, and raised the minimum margin requirement for short selling to 150% from 130% to discourage traders from taking speculative short positions.

The stabilization fund said Taiwanese market fundamentals remain strong and selling by foreign investors has gradually subsided.

In China, the three main stock exchanges said over the weekend that they will cut the minimum requirement for margin financing to 80% from 100% effective Nov. 30.

The move is aimed at helping moderately increase leverage, improve market liquidity, and promote stable, healthy market development, the operators said.

According to Chinese state media outlet Xinhua, the adjustment could theoretically free up nearly 400 billion yuan, or roughly $60 billion, in incremental funds.
